nameStory: The 'nursery' in nursery bittercress refers to its common appearance in garden centers and nurseries, where it often hitchhikes in potted plants from around the world. The 'bittercress' part comes from the peppery, slightly bitter taste of its leaves, which is characteristic of plants in the mustard family. Its scientific name 'occulta' means 'hidden,' reflecting how this small plant often goes unnoticed despite being widely spread by human activity.
description: Nursery bittercress is a small, delicate annual or biennial herb that rarely grows taller than 6-8 inches. It has tiny white flowers with four petals arranged in a cross pattern, typical of the mustard family, and small compound leaves that are divided into several leaflets. This inconspicuous plant forms small rosettes or upright stems and produces slender seed pods that can explosively scatter seeds when touched. Despite its diminutive size, it's surprisingly hardy and can pop up almost anywhere disturbed soil is found.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers, usually less than 1/8 inch across, with four petals arranged in a perfect cross pattern - a hallmark of the mustard family

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small compound leaves divided into 3-7 rounded leaflets, feeling smooth and slightly succulent to the touch, with a mild peppery taste when chewed

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Slender, upright seed pods (called siliques) that split explosively when ripe, shooting seeds several feet away with an audible pop when disturbed

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low rosettes or small upright stems, rarely exceeding 8 inches tall, with a delicate, almost wispy appearance that sways easily in the breeze

habitat: In New England, nursery bittercress is most commonly found in disturbed soils around gardens, nurseries, greenhouses, and urban areas where potted plants are grown or sold. It thrives in moist, rich soils and can appear in flower beds, along walkways, or in the cracks of pavement. This non-native species prefers partially shaded to sunny locations and often establishes itself wherever soil has been recently disturbed or imported.

seasonality.spring: Plants emerge from seeds and begin rapid growth, with small rosettes of compound leaves forming. Early flowers may appear in late spring on mild days.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering period with tiny white cross-shaped flowers blooming continuously. Seed pods develop and begin their explosive dispersal by mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Late-season plants may still be flowering and setting seed, especially in protected areas. Seeds from summer pods germinate to form new rosettes for overwintering.
seasonality.winter: Some plants persist as small green rosettes close to the ground, remaining semi-active during mild winter periods and ready to resume growth in spring.

funFact: Nursery bittercress has one of the most explosive seed dispersal mechanisms in the plant world - its ripe seed pods can launch seeds up to 10 feet away with enough force to make an audible popping sound, which is why gardeners often hear mysterious 'pops' when walking through their gardens on warm days!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with hairy bittercress, but nursery bittercress has smooth, hairless leaves while hairy bittercress has distinctly fuzzy, hairy foliage. Memory trick: if the leaves feel smooth as silk, it's likely nursery bittercress; if they feel like velvet, it's hairy bittercress.
contextualKnowledge: This species is native to Asia but has become a successful global hitchhiker, spreading primarily through the horticultural trade in potted plants and soil. In New England, it's a relatively recent arrival that's still expanding its range, making each sighting noteworthy for tracking its establishment in our region.
compareHints: Among New England's bittercresses, nursery bittercress is distinguished by its completely smooth leaves and preference for disturbed garden soils. Hairy bittercress has fuzzy leaves, while Pennsylvania bittercress grows much taller and prefers wetter, more natural habitats. The explosive seed pods are shared with other bittercresses, but nursery bittercress tends to be smaller overall than most of its relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's toothworts and bittercresses, two-leaved toothwort is unique for its simple three-parted leaves and paired leaf arrangement.
Among New England's bittercresses, hairy bittercress is distinguished by its small size, annual habit, and compound leaves with rounded leaflets.

Among its bittercress relatives, narrow-leaved bittercress stands out for its particularly slender, lance-shaped leaflets—much narrower than the rounded leaflets of hairy bittercress or the broader segments of Pennsylvania bittercress.
Among New England's bittercresses, Pennsylvania bittercress stands out for its smooth leaves and taller stature.
Among New England's toothworts, cut-leaved stands out with its three deeply-divided leaves arranged in a whorl, while two-leaved toothwort has just two broader, less-divided leaves.
Among its Cardamine relatives in New England, cuckooflower stands out for preferring wetter habitats than most bittercresses and toothworts.
Among its many Cardamine relatives in New England, bulbous cress stands out for its underground bulb and preference for very wet soils.
Large toothwort differs from its close relative cut-leaved toothwort by having more finely divided, almost lacy leaflets and typically growing taller.
Among its bittercress relatives, sand bittercress is distinguished by its preference for sandy, dry soils and its particularly small size.

Alpine bittercress is dramatically different from its lowland Cardamine relatives in New England - while species like hairy bittercress and Pennsylvania bittercress are weedy annuals that pop up in gardens and disturbed areas, alpine bittercress is a specialized perennial that grows only in extreme mountain conditions.

Long's Bittercress differs from its relatives by having the most finely divided leaves in the genus - almost thread-like compared to the broader leaflets of Two-leaved Toothwort or the simpler leaves of Hairy Bittercress.

Among its Cardamine relatives in New England, Purple Cress is unique for its potential purple flower coloration - species like Two-leaved Toothwort and the various bittercresses typically stick to white or pale pink flowers.

Among the Cardamine genus in New England, white cuckoo bitter-cress has the most finely divided, feathery leaves - much more delicate than the broader leaflets of toothworts or the simpler leaves of other bitter-cresses.
Chinese Ivy differs from other Cardamine species in New England by being strictly aquatic and having a trailing, mat-forming growth habit.
